newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco spokesman says cigarette addiction overblown.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco spokesman says cigarette addiction overblown.

text.p: The tobacco industry's chief spokesman dismissed as overblown and unfounded medical and anti-smoking claims that cigarettes are addictive, jurors in a landmark secondhand-smoke trial heard on Tuesday.

"It's sort of an overworked term .... (People say) 'I'm a videoholic. I'm a chocoholic'," Samuel Chilcote, president of the Tobacco Institute, an industry trade group, said in testimony read aloud to jurors.
"My wife has quit. I've known a lot of people who've quit," Chilcote said.

Chilcote, head of the Tobacco Institute since 1981, testified during pretrial questioning in November 1993, and also said the links between smoking and diseases such as lung cancer were not yet proven and that secondhand smoke was not a health danger.
His organization, funded by U.S. cigarette makers, is a defendant in the secondhand-smoke trial now in its third month in a Miami courtroom.

An estimated 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants are suing the tobacco industry for $5 billion, claiming their illnesses were caused by passengers smoking aboard U.S. airliners before 1990. They also accuse the companies of conspiring to hide the dangers of secondhand smoke.

The tobacco companies deny the conspiracy charges and say the incidence of lung cancer, emphysema and other tobacco-related disorders among the flight attendants was no higher than that of the general population.

Lawyers for the flight attendants are winding up their case but attorneys defending the seven tobacco companies, the Tobacco Institute and the Council for Tobacco Research Inc. were not expected to begin calling witnesses until after the Labor Day weekend ending Sept. 2. The trial began with jury selection on June 2.
